newsitem.title: CHINA: China drought threatens Yellow River.
newsitem.headline: China drought threatens Yellow River.

text.p: The Yellow River, China's second longest river, is expected to experience a record dry period this year because of drought and increased water demand, the Xinhua news agency said on Tuesday.
Hydroelectric plants on the lower reaches of the river had reported that water volumes in the first seven months of this year were 50 percent lower than in previous years, Xinhua said.
Lack of water threatened up to 52 million people and more than 7.4 million hectares (18.3 million acres) of arable land, it said.

The lower reaches of the Yellow River, once known for its devastating floods, had dried up for extended periods in each of the last six years because of drought in northern China, Xinhua said. Last year, the river dried up for a record 136 days.

Last week, State media said water had begun to flow again in a stretch of the Yellow River in eastern Shandong province, but Xinhua said much of the river was likely to remain dry for even longer than in 1996.
"The record is likely to be broken in the next two days because there will not be enough rain to cause the resumption of the flow of water on the lower reaches," Xinhua quoted an expert as saying.
Increasing water demand from provinces on the lower reaches had also contributed to the shortage, it said.
While drought and high temperatures have been plaguing northern China, floods have wreaked havoc in the south.
Devastating floods have killed 284 people in eastern and southern China so far this year, international aid workers and Chinese officials have said.
Flooding is an ancient curse across much of southern China, where summer rains can burst river dikes and inundate towns, cities and huge swathes of farmland.
